settings.heading: Twenty years in medicine. One hour in a circle in Portugal.
settings.text: I'm Holly Baynes, a pediatric nurse practitioner in Omaha, a cacao facilitator, and the founder of HHaven.

I've spent twenty years in medicine, fifteen of them in heart surgery. I still practice, and I love the work.

A few years ago, I sat in a women's circle at a retreat in Portugal. We each drew a guidance card, journaled about it, and then talked. I remember wondering what sitting in a circle was going to do. It was relaxing, and it was nice to be with other people. I wasn't expecting much more than that.

I didn't know what my card meant, so I just started writing. Afterward I read the longer description in the book that goes with the cards. It brought me right back to a time in my life I had already written about. It was a full circle moment, and I couldn't believe it was coming up.

For a while I'd been drawn to holistic practices, and I worried people thought I was weird. I kept asking, God, am I on the right track? That hour felt like an answer. Then we opened the circle up to talk. I heard so much of my own story in what the other women shared.

All of that came from one hour of sitting together, journaling, and listening to one another. Cacao became part of it on that same trip, when a woman handed me a cup.

So I learned the plant the way I learned medicine. Where it grows, what's in it, how it's made, and how much is enough. I found farmers in Peru and Brazil I trust. Now I hold circles here in Nebraska, so other people can have that hour too.

settings.quote: "It was simply sitting together, journaling, and listening to one another. The magic that comes from that community is life changing."
settings.context: On the women's circle in Portugal that started all of this.

settings.heading: What the hardest days taught me
settings.text:
I went into medicine because I wanted to help people, and I've always loved working with kids. They still have a kind of whimsy and magic in how they think. I loved the science too. If I do this, it will help you, and it's proven.

Then I started working in the ICU. I saw children we couldn't make better, and circumstances that were heartbreaking. I still do. I was following every rule. We had done the research. It was supposed to work. In my twenties, it was hard to accept that I couldn't fix it.

When I had children of my own, I saw them in my patients. I started asking what I was really there to give. Medicine and surgery matter. So does what one person gives another in the room.

Some of the memories I hold closest are of families who lost a child. Even in that much pain, they found grace. They thanked us for knowing their child, and they made us part of their story. It still astonishes me.

Medicine also taught me to trust a feeling. Good providers know it: something is wrong before any test shows it. Becoming a mother made that feeling stronger. It isn't data, and I started wondering what else is like it.

That question led me to ancient practices. They gave me a sense of awe and wholeness I hadn't found in numbers. I'm grateful for every test, technology, and surgery we have. I don't think we have to choose. I believe we need both to be well.

settings.heading: What I hold to
settings.intro: The standards behind every block and every gathering.

settings.title: Say less, and be right
settings.text: I teach what's in the cup, not what it will do for you. If I can't stand behind a claim, it doesn't go on the label.

settings.title: Listen first
settings.text: The most important thing I give anyone is my attention. That started at the bedside and it carries into every circle.

settings.title: We need both
settings.text: Modern medicine and ancient practices each give us something. I bring them together.

settings.heading: What's next
settings.text: I'm building HHaven Wellness & Social Club, a place to gather here in Nebraska. You can follow along, or join as a founding member.
